teaser: No bank, no bridge, no horizon. Just the surface of a pond at the second the wind drops.
review_notes:
Monet's remark that the lilies are only the accompaniment and the mirror of water changing at every moment is the real motif: paraphrased from an interview, check source.
1909 exhibition 'Les Nymphéas: Séries de paysages d'eau' at Durand-Ruel with 48 paintings; postponed from 1907 and 1908.
Monet destroying canvases before the show: widely reported, number left vague.
1908 letter calling the water landscapes an obsession beyond an old man's strength (to Gustave Geffroy): paraphrased.
Commercial success of the 1909 show: check.
AIC: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection, entered the museum in 1933. Dimensions approx. 89.9 x 94.1 cm.

lesson.text: The breeze has just died. For a few seconds the pond lies flat as glass, and everything above it drops onto the surface: a pale patch of sky, the dark mass of trees on the far bank. In a moment a ripple will smear it all. This canvas holds the second before.

Monet said the lilies were only the accompaniment. His real subject was the mirror of the water, whose look changed at every instant with the bits of sky reflected in it. That explains the strange choice he made here in 1906.

He pointed his eyes downward and cut out everything else. There is no shore, no bridge, no line where water meets land. A traditional landscape gives you ground to stand on and a horizon to measure by. This one gives you neither.

The canvas is almost square, about 90 by 94 centimeters (35 by 37 inches). Landscapes were normally wide rectangles. A square has no built-in direction, which suits a picture with no up-there and no far-away.
So how do you know you are looking across a pond and not at a flat blue wall? Monet leaves two sets of clues, and they pull in opposite directions.
Two kinds of marks, two kinds of space.

lines.label: A far island
lines.text: This raft of lily pads is squeezed into a thin horizontal band. You are seeing it at a low angle, from a distance.

lines.label: The near pads
lines.text: Down here the pads are scattered, rounder and larger, each one separate. They are close to your feet. The change in shape from bottom to top creates the distance.

lines.label: Straight down
lines.text: These dark, upright streaks are trees, reflected. Reflections do not recede. They plunge, so the water also reads as a depth below the surface.

lesson.text: The pads say the water runs away from you. The reflections say it goes down, and the sky in it says it goes up. Your eye keeps switching between the three. The picture never quite settles, and that is why it feels alive.
By removing the horizon, Monet made a landscape where surface, depth and sky all share one sheet of water.

Monet wrote to a friend in 1908 that these landscapes of water and reflections had become an obsession, and that the task was beyond the strength of an old man. He was sixty-seven and painting the pond almost every day.
Against all that drifting blue and violet, he needed anchors, small things that sit unmistakably on top of the water. Three areas do that job, each in its own way.

lesson.title: What floats
lesson.text: Follow the camera to the things that pin the surface down.

spots.title: Red blossoms
spots.text: Three or four flowers in pink and scarlet, each with a short dark reflection below it. They are the warmest points in a cool painting, and your eye lands here first.

spots.title: The left cluster
spots.text: A dense group of pads cut off by the edge of the canvas, with magenta flowers among them. The cropping suggests the pond carries on beyond the frame.

spots.title: Pads in outline
spots.text: Near the bottom, some pads are just a looping stroke of light green, an oval drawn with the brush, with blue water showing inside.

lesson.text: Monet worked on canvases like this for years, far longer than the instant they show. He would start outdoors at the pond, then keep adjusting in the studio. Many never satisfied him, and he destroyed a number of them with his own hands.

That is why an exhibition planned for 1907 was postponed, twice. It finally opened in Paris in May 1909 with forty-eight pond paintings, under a title he chose himself: “Water Lilies: Series of Water Landscapes.” It was a success, and the pictures sold quickly.
This canvas went to an American lumber heir, Martin A. Ryerson of Chicago, one of Monet's most loyal overseas buyers. It entered the Art Institute of Chicago with his collection in 1933.

quiz.question: What did Monet consider the real subject of his pond paintings?
options: The mirror of the water and its changing reflections
quiz.explanation: He called the lilies only the accompaniment.

quiz.question: What is unusual about the way this landscape is framed?
options: It has no horizon or bank
quiz.explanation: Monet looks down at the water and leaves out the shore.

quiz.question: What do the dark upright streaks in the middle of the canvas represent?
options: Reflections of trees on the bank
quiz.explanation: The trees themselves are outside the frame, and only their reflection appears.

quiz.question: How does Monet suggest that the top lily pads are farther away?
options: He paints them as thin horizontal bands
quiz.explanation: Distant rafts of pads are flattened into narrow strips.

quiz.question: How many pond paintings were shown in the 1909 exhibition?
quiz.explanation: The show opened in May 1909 with forty-eight canvases.

facts.text: Monet finished each of these pond paintings in a few seconds, as fast as the moment it shows.
facts.explanation: He worked on them for years, outdoors and in the studio.

facts.text: The 1909 exhibition opened exactly on schedule.
facts.explanation: It had been planned for 1907 and was postponed twice.
